# Broca’s area, variation and taxic diversity in early Homo from Koobi Fora (Kenya)

## Authors

- Amélie Beaudet<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-9363-5966](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9363-5966)) †
- Edwin de Jager<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0003-3199-8566](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3199-8566))

### Affiliations

1. Laboratoire de Paléontologie, Évolution, Paléoécosystèmes et Paléoprimatologie (PALEVOPRIM), UMR 7262 CNRS & University of Poitiers Poitiers France ([ROR:04xhy8q59](https://ror.org/04xhy8q59))
2. Department of Archaeology, University of Cambridge Cambridge United Kingdom ([ROR:013meh722](https://ror.org/013meh722))
3. School of Geography, Archaeology and Environmental Studies, University of the Witwatersrand Johannesburg South Africa ([ROR:03rp50x72](https://ror.org/03rp50x72))

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

Because brain tissues rarely fossilize, pinpointing when and how modern human cerebral traits emerged in the hominin lineage is particularly challenging. The fragmentary nature of the fossil material, coupled with the difficulty of characterizing such a complex organ, has been the source of long-standing debates. Prominent among them are the uncertainties around the derived or primitive state of the brain organization in the earliest representatives of the genus Homo, more particularly in key regions such as the Broca’s area. By revisiting a particularly well-preserved fossil endocast from the Turkana basin (Kenya), here we confirm that early Homo in Africa had a primitive organization of the Broca’s area ca. 1.9 million years ago. Additionally, our description of KNM-ER 3732 adds further information about the variation pattern of the inferior frontal gyrus in fossil hominins, with implications for early Homo taxic diversity (i.e. one or two Homo species at Koobi Fora) and the nature of the mechanisms involved in the emergence of derived cerebral traits.

## Introduction

The modern human brain is an exceptionally complex, highly specialized, and extremely costly machinery. Because of the fragmentary nature of the hominin fossil record, assessing when and how changes in the brain of our ancestors happened, and inferring any related functional, behavioral, and metabolic consequences, is particularly challenging (Zollikofer and De León, 2013). Nonetheless, reconstructing the chronological and taxonomical context of the emergence of derived cerebral traits is a prerequisite for disentangling underlying evolutionary processes. For instance, local reorganization of specific areas in an overall primitive hominin brain would support a mosaic-like evolutionary pattern (e.g. Holloway et al., 2004), and raise essential questions on the role of selection pressure (or absence of; rev. in Beaudet, 2021). Beyond the value of such information on the origins of the human brain, the assumption that Homo developed a uniquely complex brain organization (e.g. Tobias, 1987) requires further evidence.

Although brains rarely fossilize, it is possible to glean structural information about the evolutionary history of the hominin brain by studying sulcal imprints in fossil brain endocasts (Neubauer, 2014). In this regard, the Broca’s area has been the focus of much interest in paleoneurology due to striking structural differences between extant human and chimpanzee brains and endocasts, and the implication of this area in articulated language (rev. in Beaudet, 2017). Ponce de León et al., 2021 thoroughly examined brain endocasts of Homo specimens in eastern Africa and Eurasia and demonstrated that the organization of the Broca’s area in the earliest representatives of the genus before 1.5 Ma was primitive. Because the imprints of the Broca’s cap in endocasts are not always readable, they used the coronal suture and surrounding sulcal imprints as a proxy to identify frontal lobe expansion (i.e. derived condition). Unfortunately, in some of the oldest and key specimens from Africa that could represent the >1.5 Ma condition (e.g. KNM-ER 1470) the interpretations remained inconclusive.

Testing the hypothesis of Ponce de León et al., 2021 of a primitive brain in the earliest representatives of the genus Homo before 1.5 Ma thus necessitates (i) an excellent preservation of very fine neuroanatomical details in fossil endocasts, and (ii) reliable information on their taxonomic identity (i.e. Homo) and stratigraphic context (i.e. before/after 1.5 Ma). The hominin specimen KNM-ER 3732 from Kenya, which fulfills these requirements, has the potential to shed new light on this conundrum. KNM-ER 3732 was discovered during the 1974–1975 field program in the Koobi Fora Formation (area 115), east of Lake Turkana in Kenya (Leakey, 1976; Wood, 1991). KNM-ER 3732 consists of a calotte, left zygoma, and a natural endocast. The expanded neurocranium and robust upper face support an attribution to Homo sp. indet. (Wood, 1991). The specimen was lying below the KBS Tuff of the upper Burgi Member that is dated to 1.87 million years ago, which provides a minimum age (Feibel et al., 1983; Feibel et al., 2006). Accordingly, if KNM-ER 3732 shows a derived cerebral condition, the hypothesis of >1.5 Ma Homo being associated with a primitive organization of the Broca’s area is falsified. Here, we provide a comparative study of the natural endocast of the pre-1.5 Ma Homo specimen KNM-ER 3732 to test the hypothesis of a late emergence of a modern Broca’s area in the hominin lineage.

## Results

### KNM-ER 3732 offers a glimpse of early Homo prefrontal organization

The natural endocast of KNM-ER 3732, initially described by Holloway et al., 2004, preserves the dorsal part but misses the frontal pole, the occipital and temporal lobes, as well as the entire ventral surface (Figure 1). Holloway et al., 2004 estimated the endocranial volume as about 750–800 cc but pointed out the low reliability of their estimate. Wood, 1991 (Page 132) identified an ‘irregular bony excrescence on the surface of the right parietal at the level of lambda and 32 mm from the midline. It projects 6 mm from the surface of the bone, and may be an example of myositis ossificans associated with damage to the overlying temporal muscle.’ Because of the location (right parietal) and nature (traumatic) of the outgrowth, it does not affect our area of study (i.e. left frontal bone) (Walczak et al., 2015). The gyral and sulcal details are well-preserved, particularly in the prefrontal region. The superior, middle, and inferior frontal sulci are visible on both hemispheres. On the left hemisphere, the Broca’s cap is prominent. A vertical groove, identified as the precentral sulcus, separates the Broca’s cap in half (Figure 2A). On both hemispheres, the central sulcus intersects the inter-hemispheric scissure and the post-central sulcus seems to be connected to the lateral fissure. The intra-parietal sulcus can be found in the parieto-occipital region of both hemispheres. The examination of the internal surface of the braincase (Figure 2B) confirms the pattern described on the natural endocast.

Scale bar: 2 cm.

![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89054/elife-89054-fig2-v1.jpg)

**Figure 2.:** The natural endocast (A) and braincase (B) of KNM-ER 3732 are compared to the virtual endocasts of extant human (C) and chimpanzee (D) individuals. Images not to scale. ar: ascending ramus of the lateral fissure; c: central sulcus; co: coronal suture; fi: inferior frontal sulcus; fm: middle frontal sulcus; ip: intra-parietal sulcus; pc: pre-central sulcus; pt: post-central sulcus. Scale bar: 2 cm.

### KNM-ER 3732 has a primitive prefrontal cortex

When compared to extant human and chimpanzee sulcal patterns, KNM-ER 3732 closely resembles the latter (Figure 2C–D). In extant human brains and endocasts, the inferior frontal sulcus often transects the Broca’s cap, while the ascending ramus of the lateral fissure caudally borders the prominence (Figure 2C–D; Connolly, 1950; de Jager et al., 2019; de Jager et al., 2022). In chimpanzees, the central sulcus is placed more rostrally, and the inferior portion of the precentral sulcus bisects the Broca’s cap that is bordered rostrally by the inferior frontal sulcus (Figure 2E–F; Connolly, 1950; Falk et al., 2018). The coronal suture runs in between the precentral and central sulci in KNM-ER 3732, which points towards the primitive configuration described in Ponce de León et al., 2021. The sulcal pattern seen in the prefrontal cortex of KNM-ER 3732, that was detected in both the natural endocast and the inner surface of the cranium (Figure 2A–B), and more particularly the deeply marked precentral sulcus that incised the Broca’s cap, is not found in any of the early Homo specimens described in Ponce de León et al., 2021 but approximates the condition seen in the Dmanisi cranium D2282 (Fig. S1B in Ponce de León et al., 2021). However, this pattern is seen in a contemporaneous non-Homo hominin specimen in South Africa, i.e. Australopithecus sediba (Falk, 2014).

## Discussion

### Paleoneuroanatomy supports taxic diversity within early Homo

Overall, the present study not only demonstrates that Ponce de León et al.’s (2021) hypothesis of a primitive brain of early Homo cannot be rejected, but also adds information about the variation pattern of the inferior frontal gyrus. In particular, the diversity of the prefrontal sulcal patterns of hominin endocasts at Koobi Fora revives the debate about the possible presence of two early Homo species in this locality (i.e. Homo habilis sensu stricto and Homo rudolfensis). In 1983, Falk, 1983 published the description of the endocasts of two Homo specimens from Koobi Fora, KNM-ER 1470 and KNM-ER 1805. Her analysis supported the co-existence of two morphs, KNM-ER 1470 representing a more derived human-like sulcal pattern. Interestingly, cerebral evidence brought up by her analysis matched other studies that emphasized the more derived craniodental anatomy of specimens attributed to Homo rudolfensis as opposed to the more primitive (Australopithecus-like) traits identified within Homo habilis sensu stricto (Leakey et al., 2012). While describing the external morphology of the neurocranium, (Leakey, 1976: 575) noted that KNM-ER 3732 was ‘strikingly similar to KNM-ER 1470.’ This resemblance is not reflected in their cerebral organization since the present study rather suggests a primitive organization of the Broca’s cap in KNM-ER 3732. If KNM-ER 1470 had indeed a derived brain, taxic diversity as a source of variation cannot be discarded. If we go further down that route, the similarities between KNM-ER 3732 and Australopithecus sediba suggested by our study could be an argument supporting the presence of Australopithecus in Koobi Fora or the absence of a definite threshold between the two genera based on the morphoarchitecture of their endocasts (Wood and Collard, 1999).

### The evolutionary history of the human Broca’s area unraveled

Beyond the taxonomic aspect, variation detected in Koobi Fora could provide information about underlying evolutionary mechanisms, and more specifically the process of fixation of an adaptive variant, i.e. a new organization of the Broca’s area and the increase of neural interconnectivity in this region (Essen, 1997). Such neurological changes might have had deep implications for the emergence of novel behaviors, such as articulated language (Beaudet, 2017; Beaudet, 2021). Within this scenario, the study from Ponce de León et al., 2021 would suggest that this trait became stabilized by 1.5 million years ago. The identification of protracted brain growth as early as in Australopithecus afarensis (Gunz et al., 2020), inducing longer exposure to the social environment during brain maturation (rev. in Hublin et al., 2015), could be consistent with a derived organization of the Broca’s area being selected as a response to social environmental stimuli through developmental plasticity, culminating in this variant becoming dominant within Homo. In parallel, the possibility of allometric scaling and the influence of brain size on sulcal patterns in early Homo has to be further explored.

## Materials and methods

### Materials

KNM-ER 3732 is currently housed in the National Museums of Kenya in Nairobi (Kenya). We used brain and endocast atlases published in Connolly, 1950, Falk et al., 2018, and de Jager et al., 2019; de Jager et al., 2022; see also https://www.endomap.org/ for comparing the pattern identified in KNM-ER 3732 to those described in extant humans and chimpanzees. To the best of our knowledge, these atlases are the most extensive atlases of extant human and chimpanzee brains/endocasts available to date and are widely used in the literature to explore variability in sulcal patterns. In Figure 2, the extant human and chimpanzee conditions are illustrated by one extant human (adult female) and one extant chimpanzee (adult female) specimens from the Pretoria Bone Collection at the University of Pretoria (South Africa) and from the Royal Museum for Central Africa in Tervuren (Belgium), respectively (Beaudet et al., 2018).

### Digitization

Both the natural endocast and the cranium of KNM-ER 3732 were scanned using an Artec Space Spider 3D scanner and reconstructed with the software Artec Studio 16 X. The 3D mesh can be viewed on MorphoSource. The comparative specimens were imaged by microfocus X-ray tomography (Beaudet et al., 2018) at the South African Nuclear Energy Corporation in Pelindaba (South Africa) and at the Centre for X-ray Tomography of Ghent University (UGCT) in Ghent (Belgium). Virtual endocasts were generated using Endex software (Subsol et al., 2010).

### Detection and identification of sulcal imprints

Sulcal imprints were automatically detected through a geometry-based method using curvature lines computed from the natural endocast and the inner surface of the cranium. Sulcal imprints, considered as variation points of the surface on a triangle mesh, were detected through a geometry-based method using curvature lines defined as salient subsets of the extrema of the principal curvatures on surfaces (Yoshizawa et al., 2008; Beaudet et al., 2016). Vascular imprints and non-anatomical structures (e.g. fractures) were manually removed through a customized script written in MATLAB R2013a (Mathworks) that is available online (Dumoncel, 2019; https://gitlab.com/jeandumoncel/curve-editor).

# Peer review - Round 1

Editors:
- Yonatan Sahle, University of Cape Town South Africa

Reviewers:
- (Reviewers not individually listed)

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89054.3.sa0](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89054.3.sa0)

This important study uses the brain endocast of a ~1.9-million-year-old hominin fossil from Kenya, attributed to genus Homo, to show that the organization of the Broca's area in members of early Homo was primitive. Specifically, the prefrontal sulcal pattern in this early Homo specimen more closely resembles that of chimpanzees than of modern humans. Because Broca's area is associated with speech function, the compelling evidence from this study is relevant for understanding the timing and trajectory of evolution of speech related traits in our genus. Coupled with its potential implications for taxonomic classification, this study will be of interest to paleoanthropologists, paleontologists, archaeologists, and neuroscientists.

# Peer review - Round 1

Reviewers:
- Anonymous Reviewer

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89054.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89054.3.sa1)

The cerebral cortex, or surface of the brain, is where humans do most of their conscious thinking. In humans, the grooves (sulci) and bumps (convolutions) have a particular pattern in a region of the frontal lobe called Broca's area, which is important for language. Specialists study features imprinted on the internal surfaces of braincases in early hominins by casting their interiors, which produces so-called endocasts. A major question about hominin brain evolution concerns when, where, and in which fossils a humanlike Broca's area first emerged, the answer to which may have implications for the emergence of language. The researchers used advanced imaging technology to study the endocast of a hominin (KNM-ER 3732) that lived about 1.9 million years ago (Ma) in Kenya to test a recently published hypothesis that Broca's remained primitive (apelike) prior to around 1.5 Ma. The results are consistent with the hypothesis and raise new questions about whether endocasts can be used to identify the genus and/or species of fossils.

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89054.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89054.3.sa2)

The authors present new data of endocranial surface details from the early Homo specimen KNM-ER 3732 and discuss the evolution of brain surface features that might be related to the evolution of language in the hominin lineage.

Comments and issues raised by the reviewers have been addressed adequately. I am sure that this contribution will revive discussion about these issues.

# Peer review - Round 1

Reviewers:
- Anonymous Reviewer

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89054.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89054.3.sa3)

The authors provide a detailed analysis of the sulcal and sutural imprints preserved on the natural endocast and associated cranial vault fragments of the KNM-ER3732 early Homo specimen. The analyses indicate a primitive ape-like organization of this specimen's frontal cortex. Given the geological age of around 1.9 million years, this is the earliest well-documented evidence of a primitive brain organization in African Homo.

The various points raised by the reviewers and the responses provided by the authors illustrate that paleoneurology is a research field where little consensus has been reached over the past century. This is due not only to the fragmentary preservation of most fossil endocasts, but also to the limitations of scientific inference in general, and paleoneurological inference in particular. Like any scientific hypothesis, a paleoneurological hypothesis cannot be proven, but at best be falsified, leaving a wide field of possible alternative hypotheses. Furthermore, endocranial morphology does not equate cerebral morphology. A classical example: the endocranial Broca cap is not identical to the cortical Broca area. And last but not least, taxonomy cannot resolve questions of phylogeny.

results.result: KNM-ER 3732 is a well-preserved early Homo specimen from Koobi Fora, Kenya, dated to at least 1.87 Ma, with excellent preservation of sulcal details particularly in the prefrontal region. The specimen consists of a calotte, left zygoma, and natural endocast, with visible superior, middle, and inferior frontal sulci on both hemispheres, and a prominent Broca's cap on the left hemisphere bisected by the precentral sulcus.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C39 provide well-documented anatomical descriptions supported by direct observation (C20, C26, C32-C38), established citations (C19, C21-C23, C25, C27-C29), and confirmation from both the natural endocast and internal braincase surface (C39). The stratigraphic dating is properly cited and the preservation quality is directly observable in the figures.

results.result: Comparative analysis demonstrates that KNM-ER 3732 exhibits a primitive prefrontal cortex organization resembling chimpanzees rather than modern humans. The precentral sulcus bisects the Broca's cap (as in chimpanzees), and the coronal suture position indicates a primitive configuration. This pattern is not found in other early Homo specimens from Ponce de León et al. 2021 but resembles Australopithecus sediba and Dmanisi cranium D2282.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C50 are well-supported by comparative morphological data from established atlases (C41-C45), direct observations of KNM-ER 3732 (C46), and systematic comparison with published specimens (C48-C50). The use of extensive human and chimpanzee reference atlases (C70-C71) strengthens the comparative analysis. However, the comparison relies on qualitative assessment of sulcal patterns rather than quantitative metrics.

results.result: The study confirms that early Homo in Africa had a primitive organization of the Broca's area ca. 1.9 million years ago, supporting Ponce de León et al.'s (2021) hypothesis that the earliest representatives of genus Homo before 1.5 Ma possessed primitive brain organization. KNM-ER 3732 provides critical evidence that was previously inconclusive in specimens like KNM-ER 1470.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C51 represent the main conclusion supported by the anatomical observations (C40-C50) and proper hypothesis testing framework (C24). The study successfully addresses the gap identified in C17 regarding inconclusive interpretations of older specimens. The conclusion is appropriately conservative, confirming that the hypothesis 'cannot be rejected' rather than claiming definitive proof.

results.result: The diversity of prefrontal sulcal patterns among Koobi Fora specimens (particularly the contrast between KNM-ER 3732's primitive organization and KNM-ER 1470's potentially derived pattern) revives the debate about possible taxonomic diversity in early Homo at this locality, potentially supporting the presence of both Homo habilis sensu stricto and Homo rudolfensis.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C57-C58 present an interesting inference about taxonomic diversity, but the evidence is limited. The comparison relies heavily on prior work (C53-C56) and the conditional nature of C58 ('If KNM-ER 1470 had indeed a derived brain') indicates uncertainty. The inconclusive interpretation of KNM-ER 1470 noted in C17 undermines the strength of this taxonomic argument. Additional specimens and quantitative analysis would be needed to support this result.

results.result: The similarities between KNM-ER 3732 and Australopithecus sediba could indicate either the presence of Australopithecus at Koobi Fora or the absence of a definite threshold between Homo and Australopithecus based on endocast morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are highly speculative (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type) and represent alternative interpretations that are not adequately tested. The authors themselves frame this as 'if we go further down that route,' indicating this is exploratory rather than conclusive. The similarity to A. sediba is based on a single feature (precentral sulcus bisecting Broca's cap) which may not be taxonomically diagnostic. This requires substantially more evidence.

results.result: The observed variation at Koobi Fora could reflect evolutionary mechanisms involving developmental plasticity, where protracted brain growth (identified as early as Australopithecus afarensis) led to longer social exposure during maturation, potentially selecting for derived Broca's area organization through environmental stimuli, with this trait becoming stabilized by 1.5 Ma.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C67 present an evolutionary scenario that is largely speculative (C61, C63, C67 marked as SPECULATION). While the individual components are cited (C65-C66), the proposed causal chain linking protracted growth, social environment, developmental plasticity, and Broca's area reorganization is not tested or demonstrated in this study. This represents interesting hypothesis generation for future work rather than a supported result from the current data.

results.result: The influence of allometric scaling and brain size on sulcal patterns in early Homo requires further exploration.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 appropriately identifies a limitation of the current study. The authors acknowledge that allometric effects have not been adequately explored, which is an important confounding factor when comparing specimens of potentially different brain sizes. This honest assessment of what remains unknown is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: The study employed appropriate digitization methods (3D scanning for KNM-ER 3732, micro-CT for comparative specimens) and automated geometry-based sulcal detection using curvature analysis, with manual removal of non-anatomical features. Comparisons used extensive published atlases of human and chimpanzee brain morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C81 describe standard and appropriate methodological approaches. The digitization methods are well-established (C74-C77), the sulcal detection method is properly cited (C80), and the comparative materials are from recognized collections (C72-C73) using the most extensive available atlases (C71). The availability of code online (C81) supports reproducibility. However, the study lacks quantitative metrics for sulcal pattern comparison, relying instead on qualitative assessment.

results.result: The study addresses fundamental challenges in paleoneurology: brain tissues rarely fossilize, making it difficult to determine when modern human cerebral traits emerged. Studying sulcal imprints in fossil endocasts can provide structural information about brain evolution, with the Broca's area being of particular interest due to its role in language and structural differences between humans and chimpanzees.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C14 establish the scientific context and rationale for the study. These are well-established facts in paleoanthropology (C1-C5, C8-C9) supported by appropriate citations (C9, C11-C14). The logical framework connecting fossilization challenges to the importance of endocast studies (C12) and the specific focus on Broca's area (C13-C14) is sound and well-justified.

results.result: Analysis of KNM-ER 3732 demonstrates that early Homo in Africa at ~1.9 Ma had a primitive, ape-like organization of Broca's area. The sulcal pattern closely resembles chimpanzees rather than modern humans, and the coronal suture position indicates a primitive configuration, supporting the hypothesis that Broca's area remained primitive before 1.5 Ma.
results.evaluation: Multiple reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. One reviewer states the study 'show[s] that the organization of the Broca's area in members of early Homo was primitive' and describes the evidence as 'compelling.' Another reviewer confirms 'the analyses indicate a primitive ape-like organization of this specimen's frontal cortex' and notes this is 'the earliest well-documented evidence of a primitive brain organization in African Homo.' While one reviewer notes inherent limitations in paleoneurology (that hypotheses can only be falsified, not proven), no reviewer challenges the core finding.

results.result: The natural endocast of KNM-ER 3732 preserves well-defined sulcal details in the prefrontal region, including visible superior, middle, and inferior frontal sulci, a prominent Broca's cap bisected by the precentral sulcus, and other anatomical features. These observations are confirmed by examination of both the natural endocast and the internal surface of the braincase.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these observational data without challenge. One reviewer explicitly notes the authors 'provide a detailed analysis of the sulcal and sutural imprints preserved on the natural endocast and associated cranial vault fragments.' The preservation quality and anatomical observations form the foundation for the main conclusions, which reviewers support.

results.result: The distinctive sulcal pattern in KNM-ER 3732, particularly the deeply marked precentral sulcus bisecting the Broca's cap, is not found in other early Homo specimens described by Ponce de León et al. (2021) but approximates the condition in Dmanisi cranium D2282 and is seen in Australopithecus sediba.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these comparative observations. One reviewer notes the study 'adds information about the variation pattern of the inferior frontal gyrus in fossil hominins,' implicitly accepting the comparative analysis. The observations about variation are treated as contributing to broader discussions about taxonomy and evolution.

results.result: The variation in prefrontal sulcal patterns among Koobi Fora specimens, including differences between KNM-ER 3732 and KNM-ER 1470, revives debate about possible taxonomic diversity (two early Homo species) at this locality. Despite external neurocranial similarities, KNM-ER 3732 shows primitive cerebral organization unlike the potentially derived condition in KNM-ER 1470.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these implications but express caution. One reviewer notes the study 'raise[s] new questions about whether endocasts can be used to identify the genus and/or species of fossils.' Another explicitly states 'taxonomy cannot resolve questions of phylogeny,' highlighting fundamental limitations. The editor notes the study has 'potential implications for taxonomic classification' and will be 'of interest' to specialists, suggesting the taxonomic questions remain open for discussion rather than resolved.

results.result: The similarities between KNM-ER 3732 and Australopithecus sediba could support either the presence of Australopithecus at Koobi Fora or the absence of a definite threshold between Homo and Australopithecus based on endocast morphology.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly address these speculative taxonomic implications. One reviewer's statement that 'taxonomy cannot resolve questions of phylogeny' and that 'endocranial morphology does not equate cerebral morphology' suggests caution about drawing definitive taxonomic conclusions from endocast similarities. The manuscript itself presents these as speculative possibilities ('could be an argument'), and reviewers do not validate or refute them.

results.result: The observed variation in Broca's area organization could provide insights into evolutionary mechanisms, including the fixation of adaptive variants related to neural interconnectivity and language emergence. The derived organization may have been selected through developmental plasticity in response to social environmental stimuli, with stabilization occurring by 1.5 Ma.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the study's relevance for understanding 'the timing and trajectory of evolution of speech related traits' but do not explicitly validate the specific evolutionary mechanisms proposed. One reviewer emphasizes that paleoneurological hypotheses 'cannot be proven, but at best be falsified,' suggesting these evolutionary interpretations remain speculative. The editor notes the study is 'relevant for understanding' speech evolution but does not affirm the specific mechanistic proposals.

results.result: KNM-ER 3732 consists of a calotte, left zygoma, and natural endocast attributed to Homo sp. indet., dated to a minimum age of 1.87 Ma based on its stratigraphic position below the KBS Tuff. The endocast preserves the dorsal part but lacks the frontal pole, occipital and temporal lobes, and ventral surface.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these basic descriptive facts about the specimen without challenge. One reviewer explicitly notes the specimen 'lived about 1.9 million years ago (Ma) in Kenya,' accepting the dating. Another confirms the study examines 'a ~1.9-million-year-old hominin fossil from Kenya, attributed to genus Homo,' validating the attribution and age.

results.result: The study employed advanced imaging technology including 3D scanning, microfocus X-ray tomography, and automated geometry-based sulcal detection methods to analyze KNM-ER 3732 and comparative specimens.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge the methodological approach. One reviewer states 'the researchers used advanced imaging technology to study the endocast,' and another notes the authors 'provide a detailed analysis' of the specimen. No methodological concerns are raised, and one reviewer confirms that 'comments and issues raised by the reviewers have been addressed adequately,' suggesting prior methodological questions were resolved.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the main conclusion (C6, C51) that KNM-ER 3732 shows primitive ape-like organization of Broca's area. OpenEval evaluates this as SUPPORTED based on anatomical observations and proper hypothesis testing. Peer reviewers describe the evidence as 'compelling' and affirm it represents 'the earliest well-documented evidence of a primitive brain organization in African Homo.' Strong agreement on the core finding.

Both support the anatomical observations (C32-C39). OpenEval finds the anatomical descriptions well-documented through direct observation and citations. Peer reviewers accept these observational data without challenge, noting the authors 'provide a detailed analysis of the sulcal and sutural imprints.' Strong agreement on the quality and validity of anatomical observations.

Both support the comparative morphological analysis (C40-C50). OpenEval rates this SUPPORTED based on comparative data from established atlases and systematic comparison, though notes reliance on qualitative rather than quantitative assessment. Peer reviewers accept the comparative analysis as 'compelling' evidence for the main conclusion. Strong agreement despite OpenEval noting methodological limitation.

Both support the comparative observations about variation (C48-C50). OpenEval finds these well-supported by systematic comparison with published specimens. Peer reviewers accept these observations, noting the study 'adds information about the variation pattern of the inferior frontal gyrus in fossil hominins.' Agreement on the validity of comparative variation analysis.

Both express uncertainty about taxonomic diversity claims (C7, C52, C57-C58). OpenEval rates this UNCERTAIN, noting limited evidence and conditional nature of claims. Peer reviewers also express caution, stating 'taxonomy cannot resolve questions of phylogeny' and noting the study 'raise[s] new questions' rather than resolving them. Strong agreement on the uncertain nature of taxonomic implications.

Both find the A. sediba similarity claims (C59-C60) inadequately supported. OpenEval rates this UNSUPPORTED, noting it is highly speculative and based on a single feature that may not be taxonomically diagnostic. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN and do not explicitly validate these speculative possibilities, with general caution about drawing taxonomic conclusions from endocast similarities. Agreement that these claims lack sufficient support.

Both express reservations about the evolutionary mechanism claims (C61-C67). OpenEval rates this UNSUPPORTED, noting the causal chain is speculative and not tested in the study. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, emphasizing that paleoneurological hypotheses 'cannot be proven, but at best be falsified' and noting the study is 'relevant for understanding' speech evolution without affirming specific mechanisms. Agreement that these evolutionary interpretations remain speculative.

Both support the methodological approaches (C74-C81). OpenEval finds the methods standard and appropriate, with proper citations and reproducibility support, though notes lack of quantitative metrics. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the 'advanced imaging technology' and 'detailed analysis,' with no methodological concerns raised. Strong agreement on methodological validity.

Both support basic specimen facts (C20-C23, C26). OpenEval includes these in broader anatomical descriptions rated as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers accept these descriptive facts without challenge, explicitly validating the dating (~1.9 Ma) and attribution to genus Homo. Agreement on factual specimen information.

OpenEval evaluates the scientific context and rationale (C1-C14) as SUPPORTED, noting well-established facts with appropriate citations and sound logical framework. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these background/contextual claims.

OpenEval evaluates the acknowledged limitation about allometric effects (C68) as SUPPORTED, noting this honest assessment is scientifically appropriate. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses this specific limitation, though peer reviewers generally acknowledge inherent limitations in paleoneurology.
